subject: general
question: Where does the heat energy go when the solid melts but its temperature remains the same?

options.text: It is lost to the surroundings while overcoming the forces of repulsion.
It is used to overcome the forces of attraction between the particles.
It is lost to the surroundings while overcoming the forces of attraction.
It is used to overcome the forces of repulsion between the particles.

solution:
p data-end="57" data-start="0">The correct answer is __**It is used to overcome the forces of attraction between the particles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When a **solid** reaches its **melting point**, it begins to transition into a **liquid** state. During this process, even if heat is continuously supplied, the **temperature** of the substance remains **constant** until the entire solid has melted.
 
• This phenomenon occurs because the heat energy supplied is being utilized to change the **state of matter** rather than increasing the **kinetic energy** of the particles.
 
• Specifically, the energy is consumed to break the **intermolecular forces of attraction** that hold the particles in a fixed, rigid position in the **solid lattice**. ***Hence, the statement that it is used to overcome the forces of attraction is correct.***
 
• Since the **average kinetic energy** of the particles does not increase during this phase change, the **thermometer** does not show a rise in **temperature**.
 
• This "hidden" heat that is absorbed by the substance without a change in temperature is known as **Latent Heat**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Latent Heat of Fusion:**
 
 
• The **Latent Heat of Fusion** is defined as the amount of **heat energy** required to change **1 kg** of a **solid** into a **liquid** at its **melting point** at **atmospheric pressure**.
 
• For example, the latent heat of fusion for **ice** is approximately **3.34 x 10⁵ Joules per kilogram (J/kg)**. This means **3.34 x 10⁵ J** of energy is needed to convert **1 kg** of ice at **0 degree Celsius** to water at **0 degree Celsius**.
 
 
 
• **Melting Point and Pressure:**
 
 
• The **melting point** is the specific **temperature** at which a solid becomes a liquid at **1 atmospheric pressure**. For **ice**, this is **273.15 K** or **0 degree Celsius**.
 
• Different substances have different melting points based on the strength of their **chemical bonds** or **intermolecular forces**. Substances with **stronger forces of attraction** require more energy (higher temperature) to melt.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Energy Levels:**
 
 
• Particles in **water** at **0 degree Celsius** (273 K) have **more energy** as compared to particles in **ice** at the same **temperature**.
 
• This extra energy is the **latent heat** absorbed during the melting process, which allows the water particles to move more freely than the restricted particles in the ice structure.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Role of Energy in Phase Change:**
 
 
• In **Thermodynamics**, during a phase transition like **melting (fusion)** or **boiling (vaporization)**, the energy supplied goes into increasing the **potential energy** of the system rather than the **kinetic energy**.
 
• Because **temperature** is a measure of the **average kinetic energy**, the temperature remains **stagnant** during the entire duration of the state change.
 
 
 
• **Distinction between Forces:**
 
 
• The options mentioning **forces of repulsion** are scientifically inaccurate in this context. Melting is strictly about overcoming the **attractive forces** (like **Hydrogen bonding** in ice or **Ionic bonds** in salts) that keep the solid intact.
 
• Energy is not "lost" to the **surroundings** during the melting process in an ideal scenario; rather, it is **absorbed** by the substance to perform **work** against the **molecular bonds**.
